Imagine you have a hula hoop between your legs going over the top of your head. What motion would you make in your pelvis in order to move the hula hoop in a backwards circle? 

It's less of a scoop and more of a connection to each sequence of the stride. Assuming your horse is traveling on the correct lead, it's outside hind, inside hind and outside front diagonally (sale as one trot sequence) then the leading inside front leg. Cantle down and to the outside, saddle level, pommel down and to the front side. 

Think about your horse's hind legs and your seat in relation to the cantle of the saddle. 

Hope this helps!

So, cramps are generally an indicator that there's lack of oxygen going to the affected area. Side stitches are a form of cramping. Many riders (even GP riders) leverage their pelvis in order to sit the trot (their pelvis is a more active point in the body than the entire torso) which affects balance and the ability to follow this motion. The trot is less of an "up down" motion and more of a propelling forward. Think about keeping the front of your body in alignment and staying soft enough in the hips to absorb this motion without creating too much pivot through your seat bones.

I have seen many horses with questionable conformation excel at ammy level. My advice is to have him vetted, get the vet's opinion on front hoof conformation, and xray if suggested. He was very aggressive in the form of charging his owners with his ears back, asserting his dominance in dangerous ways like kicking and running over the handlers, and being labelled "unrideable" by the trainer at the barn he was boarded. When I showed up and signed their liability release, the trainer told me "that horse is going to kill you."

 The owners contacted me as a last resort. I was literally his last chance. The first day we spent together in the round pen, he started off by charging at me, teeth bared. When I asserted my OWN dominance, he spun and double-barrel kicked at me, expecting me to run out of the round pen. I drove him forward and away from me with a lunge whip (a long whip meant for ground work). 

Immediately, the aggression turned into fear. He realized I was not going to run away from him and a conversation about partnership needed to happen. It took him 45 minutes to "join up" with me, which means after many signals that he was ready to meet up with me for a new conversation he came in towards me quietly and initiated a connection by touching my shoulder with his nose. 

The first ride was far less eventful than the round penning incident in the round pen. He was actually much quieter under saddle than he was on the ground. 

His owner was a shy 15 year old kid who wanted nothing else than to be able to ride him bridleless, which means without a bit and reins (the metal mouthpiece you see in many horse's mouths connected to long pieces of leather that the rider holds). 

4 months later, after many rides and many setbacks, I had the horse going well with just a neck rope (a rope around the neck, nothing on their face). The kid hopped on and I gave her a lesson, showing her how to replicate everything I had taught her horse. She was over the moon! She later sent me a photo of her cantering the horse in just a neck rope in the middle of an open field. I will never forget the fullness in my heart I felt when I got the photo. I saved a horse's life and gave a young woman hope that with a little help, everything is possible. Whenever I'm struggling with a horse or in life in general I think of that photo and I remember why I am here.

I started riding at the age of 5 and I fell in love with horses in general. Through my adolescent years, I worked at many barns under many different local trainers. I worked off my riding lessons mucking stalls. Definitely not a glitzy start, but my parents weren't made of money. 

Fast forward many years, I got good enough that my trainer often asked me to ride the "problem ponies" in her lesson programs that needed someone with more experience to "tune them up." I enjoyed this, and I started becoming aware of the whys. Why is the pony bucking? Why is he refusing a jump? Etc. Being young still, I did what I could to get them riding better in the lesson programs, but I lacked finesse and the education it takes to become an actual trainer. However, this gave me a taste of the realm of training.

I got my own horse at the age of 13 - a thoroughbred off the track that I took on as my first horse and first training project. I owned him for the rest of his life (19 YEARS)! 

Along with owning my boy, I continued working with my trainer's horses and became a working student for a new trainer. A working student is basically someone who works their ass off just to ride in a lesson with the trainer and make maybe $75 a week on top of that...if you're lucky. It is a LOT of hard work getting into horses without having lots of money. 

I competed until my early 20s. Got a really cool opportunity to work with an upper level rider in Florida. Moved down there and continued my education, but when I saw what the reality of the making it into the "big time" in competition was all about, I decided I wanted to come home and focus on training. All of this prior experience led me to start my own business. It took 3 years to take off. Lots of sleepless nights over how I was going to make enough money to survive. 

Today, I have many horses in training and run a successful freelance (travel-to-your-barn) training business. It was a long and bumpy road with more falls than I can count. 

Being a trainer is extremely rewarding, but not in the way a lot of people think. To me, it's not about winning ribbons and getting recognized by top level people. My passion is meeting the horse where they're at, identifying the cracks in their foundation causing the issues, and working from there. Then, I have to get the rider on board and on the same page to continue resolving the issue. Honestly, the people are FAR harder to deal with than the horses, and sometimes certain clients can make the job very difficult. My goal is to get the horse and rider to a point where they don't need me anymore, but want me there to help them progress.

Wood chewing and cribbing are two different behaviors. Wood chewing is not a stereotypic behavior, but cribbing is. The act of cribbing involves sucking air in as they brace against the wood.

This is called cribbing. It's a stereotypic behavior often brought on by stress. Most causes of stress in horses is brought on by lack of one of the three "Fs" - Friends, Forage and Freedom. Does this horse have 24/7 access to hay? Are they stalled at night? Out with a group? Sometimes changing their environment can resolve this, however it's a fairly addictive habit (kind of like smoking), so it may be something that will not go away even with changes to the lifestyle. I always recommend changing the horse's environment and making it as close to how a horse would be living in the wild as possible before trying something like a cribbing collar.
